mainTopic: Taanit 4a: drizzle and the תלמיד חכם, three who asked improperly and כנסת ישראל's requests, and which תנא the משנה on asking for rain follows
overview: The amud opens at the end of a list of rain types: עורפילא, a light drizzle, helps even a seed buried under a clod of earth. רבא uses that seed image for a young תלמיד חכם, who keeps growing once he breaks through. Next come sayings about a scholar's toughness. רבא says his anger comes from the Torah's fire. רב אשי says a real scholar must be hard as iron, and רבי אבא gives another פסוק for the same idea. רבינא balances this: everyone must still train himself to be gentle. רבי יונתן then lists three people who asked improperly: אליעזר and שאול were answered well, but יפתח was answered tragically. Two verses from ירמיה comment on יפתח's sacrifice. רבי ברכיה adds that כנסת ישראל also asked improperly twice, once comparing God to rain and once asking to be a seal on His heart. Both times God answered with something better: dew, and being engraved on His palms. Finally the גמרא returns to the משנה about asking for rain. רבא says it follows רבי יהושע, while אביי says it can follow רבי אליעזר too, because asking and mentioning are separate. A second version of this discussion begins and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Drizzle helps even a seed under a clod
steps.stepSummary: עורפילא, a fine drizzle, is good even for a seed buried under a clod of earth.
steps.simpleTranslation: A drizzle is helpful even to a seed that is under a clod of earth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a list of rain types and what each one is good for. Light drizzle is praised because it reaches even buried seeds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Heavy rain could damage things or never reach a seed hidden under hard earth. A fine drizzle soaks in gently and gets everywhere. This image of a buried seed is about to be reused for a תלמיד חכם.

keyTerms.meaning: That is under a clod of earth

phrases.english: Drizzle: even to a seed
that is under a clod of earth, it is beneficial to it.
phrases.notes: This continues a list of rain types from the end of the previous amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: עוּרְפִּילָא — אֲפִילּוּ לְפַרְצִידָא דְּתוּתֵי קָלָא מַהְנְיָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of rain types from the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Light drizzle benefits even seeds buried under earth.

steps.title: What does the word for drizzle mean
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word עורפילא means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is עורפילא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask about the meaning of the unusual word it just used. This sets up a short word explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack. It is a plain question about a word. The גמרא wants to show that the word's name hints at what drizzle does.

phrases.english: What is 'urpila'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the term used in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning or origin of the word עורפילא.

steps.title: Drizzle means arise, furrows
steps.stepSummary: The word עורפילא is read as עורו פילי, meaning 'wake up, furrows'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Arise, furrows.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word is a blend of two words, עורו פילי. It means the drizzle wakes up the furrows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name itself tells you what the rain does. It soaks into the cracks in the ground and makes the seeds inside start to grow.

keyTerms.meaning: Furrows or cracks in the ground

phrases.english: 'Arise, furrows.'
phrases.notes: A wordplay that splits the word עורפילא into two parts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: עורפילא is a contraction of עורו פילי, 'arise, furrows'.

steps.title: A young scholar is like a buried seed
steps.stepSummary: רבא compares a young תלמיד חכם to a seed under a clod: once it sprouts, it keeps sprouting.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: This young Torah scholar is like a seed under a clod of earth. Once it sprouts, it keeps sprouting.
steps.whatsHappening: Because the גמרא just mentioned a seed under a clod, it brings another saying of רבא that uses the same picture. This time the picture describes a Torah scholar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A seed under hard earth takes time to break through. Once it does, it grows steadily. In the same way, a young scholar may seem slow at first, but once he breaks through, his greatness keeps increasing.

keyTerms.meaning: Once it sprouts, it keeps sprouting

phrases.english: And Rava said:
This young Torah scholar
is like a seed under a clod of earth,
since once it sprouts, it keeps sprouting.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: הַאי צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן דָּמֵי לְפַרְצִידָא דְּתוּתֵי קָלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Borrows the seed image from step 1 and applies it to a scholar.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once a young scholar breaks through, he keeps growing.

steps.title: A scholar's anger comes from the Torah's fire
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that when a תלמיד חכם gets angry, it is the Torah heating him up, based on 'My word is like fire'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: When a young Torah scholar gets heated, it is the Torah that heats him up, as it says, 'Is not My word like fire, says ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another saying of רבא about Torah scholars. It explains why scholars sometimes get angry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah is compared to fire, and fire makes things hot. So a scholar full of Torah may burn with intensity. The point is to judge his temper kindly, as a side effect of his learning.

keyTerms.meaning: Heats him up, makes him angry

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not praising anger. He is explaining where it comes from so that we judge the scholar favorably. רבינא soon adds that a person must still work on being gentle.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
This young Torah scholar who gets heated
it is the Torah that heats him up,
as it is stated: 'Is not My word like this,
like fire, says the Lord.'
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 23:29

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: הַאי צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן דְּרָתַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another saying of רבא about scholars, joined by the same theme.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A scholar's anger comes from the fiery Torah inside him.

steps.title: A true scholar must be hard as iron
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that a תלמיד חכם who is not as hard as iron is not a real scholar, based on the same verse's 'like a hammer that shatters rock'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב אשי said: Any Torah scholar who is not hard like iron is not a Torah scholar, as it says, 'And like a hammer that shatters rock.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי adds a related teaching from the second half of the same פסוק. He says firmness is part of being a real scholar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא used the 'fire' part of the פסוק. רב אשי uses the 'hammer' part. A hammer is strong and does not bend, so a scholar must stand firm in his rulings and not waver.

phrases.english: And Rav Ashi said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁאֵינוֹ קָשֶׁה כַּבַּרְזֶל —
phrases.english: Any Torah scholar who is not hard like iron
is not a Torah scholar,
as it is stated: 'And like a hammer that shatters rock.'
phrases.notes: The same פסוק, ירמיהו 23:29

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: כׇּל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁאֵינוֹ קָשֶׁה כַּבַּרְזֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the same פסוק that רבא used, from its second half.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A true scholar must be firm like iron.

steps.title: A different verse for the iron-hard scholar
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא tells רב אשי that his group learns the same idea from 'a land whose stones are iron', read as 'whose builders are iron'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said to רב אשי: You learn it from there. We learn it from here, as it is written, 'A land whose stones are iron.' Do not read 'its stones' (אבניה), but 'its builders' (בוניה).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא agrees with רב אשי's idea but brings a different פסוק as its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule stays the same: scholars must be like iron. Only the source changes. By rereading אבניה as בוניה, the פסוק teaches that the land's builders, meaning its Torah scholars, are like iron.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said to Rav Ashi:
You learn it from there.
We learn it from here,
as it is written: 'A land whose stones are iron.'
phrases.notes: דברים 8:9

phrases.english: Do not read 'its stones,'
but rather 'its builders.'
phrases.notes: The builders are the Torah scholars, who build the world spiritually.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתּוּן, מֵהָתָם מַתְנִיתוּ לַהּ. אֲנַן, מֵהָכָא מַתְנֵינַן לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different פסוק as the source for רב אשי's idea.
steps.raayaObject: That a תלמיד חכם must be as hard as iron.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 8:9, 'ארץ אשר אבניה ברזל', read as 'בוניה'.

steps.title: Even so, train yourself to be gentle
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says that even with all this, a person must teach himself to act gently, as it says, 'Remove anger from your heart.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Even so, a person must teach himself to act gently, as it says, 'And remove anger from your heart...'
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא balances the earlier teachings. Firmness and Torah fire are real, but they do not give anyone permission to be angry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier sayings could be misread as approving of a harsh temper. רבינא makes it clear that a person must still work on himself to be calm and gentle. A scholar can be firm in his learning and still be gentle in how he acts.
steps.whatToRemember: A תלמיד חכם may burn with Torah and must stand firm like iron. Even so, every person has to train himself to be gentle and remove anger from his heart.

phrases.english: Ravina said: Even so,
a person is required
to teach himself to act gently,
as it is stated: 'And remove anger from your heart, etc.'
phrases.notes: קהלת 11:10

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits and balances the praise of a scholar's toughness in steps 5 to 7.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Toughness in Torah does not excuse anger. A person must train himself to be gentle.

steps.title: Three who asked improperly
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן teaches that three people asked God improperly. Two got a good answer and one got a bad answer: אליעזר עבד אברהם, שאול בן קיש, and יפתח הגלעדי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: Three people asked improperly. Two were answered properly, and one was answered improperly. They are: אליעזר the servant of אברהם, שאול son of קיש, and יפתח the Gileadite.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new teaching. It lists three people who made risky requests of God. This sets up a later statement by רבי ברכיה about a request involving rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of the three made a request or vow that could have ended badly. With אליעזר and שאול, God arranged a good outcome. With יפתח, the bad possibility actually happened. The details of each case come in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.whyThisMatters: This list prepares for רבי ברכיה's teaching that כנסת ישראל also asked improperly, using a rain image, and was answered properly. That keeps the topic tied to rain in מסכת תענית.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
Three asked improperly,
two were answered properly,
one was answered improperly.
And these are they:
Eliezer, servant of Abraham,
and Saul son of Kish, and Jephthah the Gileadite.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן: שְׁלֹשָׁה שָׁאֲלוּ שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic that leads into a later rain-related teaching.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three asked improperly. Two (אליעזר and שאול) were answered favorably, and one (יפתח) was not.

steps.title: אליעזר's open-ended request and God's good answer
steps.stepSummary: אליעזר עבד אברהם said that whichever girl gives him water will be יצחק's wife. That could have been an unfit girl, but God sent רבקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: אליעזר עבד אברהם: as it is written, 'And it shall be that the maiden to whom I say, Please tip your pitcher, etc.' This could have been even a lame girl or even a blind girl. But God answered him properly, and רבקה came to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first of רבי יונתן's three cases: אליעזר. It shows what was improper about his request and how God still gave him a good result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אליעזר set a sign: any girl who offers water is the right match for יצחק. The problem is that the sign did not screen for anything. A lame or blind girl could have passed it. Still, God answered him properly by sending רבקה, who was a perfect match.

keyTerms.meaning: asked improperly. A request that is too open-ended and could lead to a bad result
God answered him properly. God gave a fitting result
it could have been. Introduces the bad possibility the request left open

steps.confusionAlert: 'הֵשִׁיבוּ כַּהוֹגֶן' means God answered him properly. It does NOT mean that people answered אליעזר. The subject here is Heaven.

phrases.english: Eliezer, the servant of Abraham —
phrases.notes: First of the three cases listed by רבי יונתן in step 9.

phrases.english: as it is written: 'And it shall be that the maiden
phrases.notes: בראשית 24:14

phrases.english: to whom I will say,
Please tip your pitcher, etc.'
phrases.notes: The verse continues: whoever offers water to him and his camels is the one God chose for יצחק.

phrases.english: This could have been even a lame girl, even a blind girl.
phrases.notes: This is the improper part: the sign did not rule out an unsuitable match.

phrases.english: God answered him properly,
and Rebecca happened to come to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first name on רבי יונתן's list from step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אליעזר's sign was open-ended and could have brought an unfit wife, but God answered properly with רבקה.

steps.title: שאול's open-ended promise and God's good answer
steps.stepSummary: שאול בן קיש promised his daughter to whoever killed גלית. That could have been an unfit man, but God sent דוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: שאול בן קיש: as it is written, 'And it shall be that the man who strikes him down, the king will make him very rich and will give him his daughter.' This could have been even a slave or even a ממזר. But God answered him properly, and דוד came to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second case: שאול. It shows his promise was too open-ended, but it still ended well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שאול offered his daughter to anyone who killed גלית. That man could have been an עבד or a ממזר, who is not allowed to marry a regular Jewish woman. God answered properly, and the one who killed גלית was דוד.

keyTerms.meaning: a child from a forbidden union, who may not marry a regular Jewish woman
and there happened to come to him (God arranged it)

phrases.english: Saul, son of Kish —
phrases.notes: Second case on the list.

phrases.english: as it is written: 'And it shall be that the man who strikes him down,
phrases.notes: שמואל א 17:25. 'Him' refers to גלית.

phrases.english: the king will make him very rich,
and will give him his daughter.'
This could have been even a slave, even a mamzer.
phrases.notes: The improper part: the winner might have been someone who could not marry the king's daughter.

phrases.english: God answered him properly,
and David happened to come to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the same pattern as step 10 for the second name on the list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שאול's promise could have given his daughter to an unfit man, but God answered properly with דוד.

steps.title: יפתח's open-ended vow and its tragic answer
steps.stepSummary: יפתח הגלעדי vowed to offer whatever came out of his house first. That could have been an impure animal. God answered him improperly, and his daughter came out.
steps.simpleTranslation: יפתח הגלעדי: as it is written, 'And it shall be that whatever comes out of the doors of my house, etc.' This could have been even something impure. God answered him improperly: his daughter came out to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the third case: יפתח. This is the one case where the open-ended request ended badly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יפתח vowed to bring as a קרבן whatever came out of his house first. It could have been a טמא animal, which cannot be a קרבן. This time God answered 'שלא כהוגן', as a fitting response to an improper vow: his own daughter came out.

keyTerms.meaning: an impure thing, such as a non-kosher animal that cannot be a קרבן
God answered him improperly, meaning with a bad outcome

steps.whatToRemember: There are three people with open-ended requests. Two got good results (רבקה, דוד) and one got a tragic result (יפתח's daughter).

phrases.english: Jephthah the Gileadite —
phrases.notes: Third case: the one who was answered badly.

phrases.english: as it is written: 'And it shall be that whatever comes out
phrases.notes: שופטים 11:31

phrases.english: that comes out of the doors of my house, etc.'
phrases.notes: The verse continues: 'it shall be for God, and I will bring it up as an עולה.'

phrases.english: This could have been even an impure thing.
God answered him improperly,
his daughter happened to come to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The contrasting case: the same open-ended pattern as steps 10 and 11, but with a bad outcome.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יפתח's vow could have meant offering a טמא animal, and God answered him badly: his daughter came out.

steps.title: The prophet's hint that יפתח could have been helped
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא links יפתח's story to ירמיה's verse 'Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no doctor there?', hinting that his vow could have been undone.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what the prophet said to the Jewish people: 'Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no doctor there?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a verse from ירמיה and reads it as pointing back to יפתח הגלעדי. It adds a final comment to his story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'גלעד' ties the verse to יפתח הגלעדי. The 'balm' and 'doctor' hint that there was a cure available: his vow could have been released (התרת נדרים). The tragedy happened because he did not use the fix that was there.

keyTerms.meaning: and this is what is meant by. Links a verse or saying to the topic just discussed

steps.whyThisMatters: It turns יפתח's story into a lesson: the disaster could have been avoided, because a way to undo the vow existed.

phrases.english: And this is what was said to them
phrases.notes: Formula that connects a verse to the case just discussed.

phrases.english: by the prophet to the Jewish people:
phrases.notes: The prophet is ירמיה (ירמיה 8:22).

phrases.english: 'Is there no balm in Gilead?
phrases.notes: 'גלעד' points to יפתח הגלעדי.

phrases.english: Is there no doctor there?'
phrases.notes: There was a way to heal the situation: the vow could have been released.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a verse that comments on the יפתח case from step 12.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that יפתח's tragedy could have been avoided
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיה 8:22: 'Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no doctor there?'

steps.title: A second verse in ירמיה about sacrifices God never wanted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes another verse in ירמיה in which God says these sacrifices were things He never commanded, never spoke of, and never thought of.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: 'Which I did not command, and I did not speak, nor did it come into My heart.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second verse from ירמיה connected to יפתח's story. This line only quotes the verse and sets up the next step, which explains each of its three parts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ירמיה this verse is about people burning their children as offerings. The verse has three separate phrases, and the גמרא will treat each phrase as pointing to a different person. Right now the verse is just being laid out.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is written: brings another verse as support
It came into My heart (I thought of it)

phrases.english: And it is written:
"Which I did not command,
and I did not speak,
phrases.notes: ירמיה 19:5

phrases.english: nor did it come into My heart."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second verse from ירמיה, after the 'balm in Gilead' verse, that also relates to יפתח's sacrifice.
steps.raayaObject: That יפתח's sacrifice of his daughter was against God's will

steps.title: Three phrases, three sacrifices: מישע's son, יפתח, and יצחק
steps.stepSummary: Each phrase of the verse refers to a different case: 'I did not command' is בנו של מישע, 'I did not speak' is יפתח, and 'it did not come into My heart' is יצחק.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Which I did not command' is the son of מישע, king of מואב, as it says: 'He took his firstborn son, who would reign after him, and offered him as a burnt offering.' 'And I did not speak' is יפתח. 'Nor did it come into My heart' is יצחק son of אברהם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the verse phrase by phrase and matches each phrase to one person who was offered, or almost offered, as a sacrifice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מישע's son was something God never commanded at all. יפתח's daughter was something God never spoke about, since יפתח made the vow on his own. With יצחק, God did command it, but He never actually intended for יצחק to be killed. It was only a test.

keyTerms.meaning: מישע, king of מואב, who sacrificed his son (מלכים ב 3:27)
And he offered him up as a burnt offering
As it is said: introduces a verse

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think God never commanded the עקידה. He did command it. The point is that He never intended for it to actually be carried out. That is why יצחק matches 'it did not come into My heart' and not 'I did not command'.

phrases.english: "Which I did not command":

phrases.aramaic: זֶה בְּנוֹ שֶׁל מֵישַׁע מֶלֶךְ מוֹאָב,
phrases.english: this is the son of Mesha, king of Moab,
as it is said: "He took his firstborn son
who would reign in his place
and offered him up as a burnt offering."
"And I did not speak": this is Yiftach;
"Nor did it come into My heart":
this is Yitzchak, son of Avraham.
phrases.notes: God commanded the עקידה only as a test, never intending it to happen.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲשֶׁר לֹא צִוֵּיתִי זֶה בְּנוֹ שֶׁל מֵישַׁע מֶלֶךְ מוֹאָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the three phrases of the verse quoted in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three phrases refer to three sacrifices: מישע's son (never commanded), יפתח's daughter (never spoken of), and יצחק (never intended).

steps.title: רבי ברכיה: the Jewish people also asked improperly, asking God to come like rain
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברכיה adds that כנסת ישראל also asked God improperly, by asking Him to come 'like the rain', and yet God answered properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ברכיה said: כנסת ישראל also asked improperly, and the הקב"ה answered her properly, as it says: 'Let us know, let us eagerly pursue knowing ה׳. His coming is as sure as the dawn, and He will come to us like the rain.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ברכיה adds one more case to רבי יונתן's list of improper requests: the whole Jewish people. This step lays out the improper request, and the next step gives God's proper answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אף' (also) ties this case to the earlier ones (אליעזר, שאול, יפתח). The improper part is comparing God's closeness to rain, since rain is not always a good thing. This brings the sugya back to its main topic of rain.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי ברכיה, the Amora making this statement
The Congregation of Israel: the Jewish people as a whole
Improperly, not as it should be

phrases.english: Rabbi Berechya said:

phrases.aramaic: אַף כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שָׁאֲלָה שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן,
phrases.english: The Congregation of Israel also asked improperly,
and the Holy One, Blessed be He, answered her properly,
as it is said: "Let us know, let us eagerly strive to know ה׳;
His coming is as sure as the dawn,
and He will come to us like the rain."
phrases.notes: הושע 6:3. Comparing God to rain is the 'improper' request.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי בֶּרֶכְיָה אַף כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שָׁאֲלָה שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a fourth case to רבי יונתן's list of improper requests and brings the topic back to rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: כנסת ישראל asked improperly by comparing God to rain, yet God answered properly.

steps.title: God's answer: I will be like dew, which is always wanted
steps.stepSummary: God tells the Jewish people that rain is sometimes wanted and sometimes not, so He will instead be to them like dew, which is always wanted.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הקב"ה said to her: My daughter, you are asking for something that is sometimes wanted and sometimes not wanted. But I will be for you something that is always wanted, as it says: 'I will be like the dew to Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: This step gives God's proper answer to the improper request from the previous step. It completes רבי ברכיה's first example, and the next step brings a second one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rain can be harmful, for example when it falls out of season, so it is not always a blessing. Dew comes in every season and is always good. God switches the comparison from rain to dew, which is why His answer counts as 'proper'.

keyTerms.meaning: My daughter: God's loving way of addressing the Jewish people

steps.whatToRemember: The list of improper requests has four cases. אליעזר and שאול were answered well, and יפתח was answered badly. רבי ברכיה adds כנסת ישראל, which asked for God to come like rain (sometimes unwanted). God answered properly that He will be like dew, which is always a blessing.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ties the aggadic list back to the daf's main topic of rain. It also teaches that rain is not always a blessing, while dew always is.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to her:
My daughter, you are asking for something
that is sometimes wanted
and sometimes is not wanted,
phrases.notes: Rain, for example in the summer, is not wanted.

phrases.english: but I will be for you
something that is always wanted,
as it is said: "I will be like the dew to Israel."
phrases.notes: הושע 14:6

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בִּתִּי אַתְּ שׁוֹאֶלֶת דָּבָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives God's proper answer to the improper request quoted in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God replaces the 'rain' comparison, which is sometimes unwanted, with 'dew', which is always wanted.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Even when the Jewish people asked improperly, God answered with a blessing that is always good.

steps.title: The Jewish people ask to be a seal on God's heart and arm
steps.stepSummary: Continuing רבי ברכיה's teaching, כנסת ישראל makes a second less-than-ideal request: to be set like a seal on God's heart and arm.
steps.simpleTranslation: And she also asked in an improper way. She said before Him: 'Master of the World! Set me as a seal on Your heart, as a seal on Your arm.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ברכיה gives a second example of כנסת ישראל asking God for something in a way that was not ideal. Here she asks to be like a seal on God's heart and arm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same pattern as the rain request in Step 16. The request is loving, but it picks an image that has a weakness. That weakness will be spelled out in God's answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Not properly / not in the ideal way
A seal or signet (worn on the body as a sign of closeness)

phrases.english: And she also asked improperly,
phrases.notes: 'She' = כנסת ישראל, continuing from Step 16.

phrases.english: she said before Him: Master of the World!
'Set me as a seal upon Your heart,
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 8:6

phrases.english: as a seal upon Your arm.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second example to the rain-versus-dew example in Steps 16-17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: כנסת ישראל asked to be a seal on God's heart and arm, which was another request that was not ideal.

steps.title: God answers: engraved on My palms, which are always seen
steps.stepSummary: God explains that a seal on the heart or arm is sometimes visible and sometimes not, so He will engrave her on His palms, which are always visible.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to her: 'My daughter, you are asking for something that is sometimes seen and sometimes not seen. But I will make for you something that is seen always, as it says: "Behold, I have engraved you on My palms."'
steps.whatsHappening: God answers the request from Step 18. He says a seal on the heart or arm can be covered by clothing, so He gives her something better: being engraved on His palms, which are always visible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The flaw in the request is that the heart and arm are often covered, so the seal is not always seen. God answers 'properly' by giving a version that is permanent. This matches the rain-versus-dew lesson: God gives something constant instead of something that comes and goes.

keyTerms.meaning: My daughter (God's loving address to כנסת ישראל)

steps.whatToRemember: Both examples (rain or dew, and arm or palm) teach the same idea: even when כנסת ישראל asks in an imperfect way, God answers with something constant and lasting.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to her:
My daughter, you are asking for a thing
that is sometimes seen and sometimes not seen,
phrases.notes: The heart and arm are usually covered by clothing.

phrases.english: but I will make for you
a thing that is always seen,
as it says: 'Behold, I have engraved you on the palms.'
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 49:16

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives God's improved answer to the request in Step 18 and closes the אגדה section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Instead of a seal that is sometimes seen, God engraves Israel on His palms, which are always seen.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: which תנא says we ask for rain only near the rainy season?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה 'אין שואלין את הגשמים', assumes that asking and mentioning rain are the same thing, and asks which תנא the משנה follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'We do not ask for rain' and so on. They assumed that asking and mentioning are one and the same thing. Who is the תנא of this משנה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the אגדה and goes back to the משנה, which says we only ask for rain close to the rainy season. Working from the assumption that asking and mentioning are the same, it asks which תנא this fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי אליעזר said we start mentioning rain on the first day of סוכות, and רבי יהושע said on the last day. If 'asking' is the same as 'mentioning', then 'only close to the rainy season' sounds like the later date. That would match only one of the two opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: Requesting rain (asking for it, as in 'ותן טל ומטר')
Mentioning rain (praising God as the one who brings it, as in 'משיב הרוח')
Who is the תנא (which Sage does this teaching follow)?

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up שאלה and הזכרה. שאלה is actually asking for rain. הזכרה is only mentioning God's power over rain. The whole discussion depends on whether these are one thing or two.

phrases.english: 'We do not ask for rain' and so on.
phrases.notes: Quoting the משנה: '...except close to the rainy season.'

phrases.english: They assumed: asking and mentioning
are one and the same thing,
who is the Tanna?

steps.triggerLanguage: סַבְרוּהָ: שְׁאֵלָה וְהַזְכָּרָה חֲדָא מִילְּתָא הִיא, מַאן תַּנָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new section: the גמרא returns from the אגדה to analyzing the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא's opinion matches the משנה's rule that we ask for rain only close to the rainy season, assuming asking and mentioning are the same?

steps.title: רבא: The משנה follows רבי יהושע
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the משנה follows רבי יהושע, who says we begin mentioning rain at the time the לולב is put down.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is רבי יהושע, who said we begin from the time it (the לולב) is put down.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question from Step 20. He says the משנה follows רבי יהושע, who starts mentioning rain on שמיני עצרת, when we stop taking the לולב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא keeps the assumption that asking and mentioning are the same thing. According to רבי יהושע, the starting date is שמיני עצרת, which really is close to the rainy season. So it fits the משנה's words 'only close to the rains.'

keyTerms.meaning: From the time it is put down (the לולב, meaning שמיני עצרת)
An אמורא who answers the question

phrases.english: Rava said: It is Rabbi Yehoshua,
who said: from the time of its putting down.
phrases.notes: 'Its' = the לולב, which is no longer taken on שמיני עצרת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה follows רבי יהושע, whose starting date (שמיני עצרת) is close to the rainy season.

steps.title: אביי: It could even follow רבי אליעזר, since asking and mentioning are separate
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the משנה can fit even רבי אליעזר, because asking for rain and mentioning rain are two separate things with different start dates.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: You can even say it is רבי אליעזר. Asking is one thing, and mentioning is a separate thing.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי pushes back on רבא's answer. He says we do not need to limit the משנה to רבי יהושע, because the starting assumption is wrong: asking and mentioning are two different things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to אביי, רבי אליעזר's 'first day of סוכות' is only about mentioning rain. Actually asking for rain can still start later, close to the rainy season. So the משנה works for both תנאים, and the assumption from Step 20 is taken apart.

keyTerms.meaning: You can even say (the משנה fits a different opinion too)
An אמורא, רבא's frequent partner in discussion

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, שאלה (asking for rain) and הזכרה (mentioning rain) are two separate things. That is why the משנה can fit both רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
You can even say it is Rabbi Eliezer —
phrases.notes: רבי אליעזר mentions rain from the first day of סוכות.

phrases.english: asking is separate, and mentioning is separate.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the need for רבא's answer by challenging the assumption behind the question.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the משנה must follow only רבי יהושע.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The question assumed that asking and mentioning are one thing. They are really separate, so רבי אליעזר's date for mentioning does not decide the date for asking.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why, in practice, we start mentioning rain (משיב הרוח) at a different time from when we start asking for it (ותן טל ומטר).

steps.title: A second version of the discussion begins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces another version of the same discussion, opening with 'Let us say...'
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say: Let us say...
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is starting a second version of the רבא and אביי discussion, and the rest of it continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ואיכא דאמרי' tells us that a different tradition reported this discussion in another way. 'לימא' introduces a suggested conclusion that the גמרא will then test. The content of the suggestion comes right on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say (introduces another version of the discussion)
Let us say (introduces a suggestion to be tested)

phrases.english: And some say: Let us say
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a second version of the discussion in Steps 20-22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Begins a suggested inference about the משנה's תנא in the alternate version. The full content continues on the next amud.
